lesson.title: Adjective Endings: the Article's Echo
lesson.subtitle: der kalte Tag vs ein kalter Tag — the adjective only speaks when the article is silent

hook.title: One Flag Per Phrase
hook.content: German grammar allows exactly ONE flag-carrier per noun phrase — one ending that shouts the case and gender. When der/die/das stands in front, the article carries the flag and the adjective falls silent-ish: der kalt**e** Tag. But ein is a quiet article — it has no ending in the masculine nominative — so the adjective must pick the flag up: ein kalt**er** Tag. That is the whole system: the adjective is the article's echo, speaking only when the article cannot. English ran this same show once — 'the olden days', 'mine host' — and then let the endings go. German never did.

footnotes.title: Predicative = No Flag At All
footnotes.content: Der Tag ist kalt — no ending, because the adjective is not INSIDE a noun phrase, it stands alone after ist. The echo only sounds before a noun: der kalte Tag, but der Tag ist kalt. English does exactly the same: 'the cold day' vs 'the day is cold'.

pattern.title: The 80/20 Echo Rule
pattern.content:
After der/die/das (the loud articles): adjective takes -e in the nominative singular and -en almost everywhere else — der kalte Tag, den kalten Tag, die kalte Nacht, das kalte Wasser. After ein/kein/mein (the quiet articles): the adjective copies the article's missing ending — ein kalt**er** Tag (masc. nom.), ein kalt**es** Wasser (neut. nom./acc.), but ein kalt**en** Tee (masc. acc.), eine kalt**e** Nacht (fem.). The 80/20: when in doubt before ANY noun in real sentences, -en is the safe echo — den kalten Tee, mit einem kalten Getränk, die kalten Hände. Pattern: der gute Wein, ein guter Wein, der alte Kaffee, ein alter Kaffee, die kleine Nacht, eine kleine Nacht.

Remember the golden boundary of this law: Predicate adjectives (adjectives that stand after 'ist/sind' rather than in front of a noun, like 'Der Kaffee ist kalt' or 'Die Suppe ist heiß') take NO ending at all — only an adjective standing directly in front of a noun wears a case/gender flag.
pattern.linguist_note: The two declensions are the living remains of the older demonstrative system: der/die/das and dieser/jener carry their own case endings (they ARE the old demonstratives), so the adjective never needs to double up. Ein is historically 'one' — a bare numeral with no flag — so the adjective is drafted to carry it.

exercises.prompt: Match each noun phrase with who carries the case flag:
exercises.target_answer: der kalte Tag, ein kalter Tag, das kalte Wasser, ein kaltes Wasser
exercises.meaning: the cold day, a cold day, the cold water, a cold water
exercises.explanation: After der/die/das the adjective rests (-e); after ein it echoes the article's missing -er/-es. lecker (delicious — lick's cousin) rests to -e after der: der leckere Kuchen; neu goes strong after ein: ein neues Auto.

exercises.prompt: 'Ich nehme ein _____ Bier.' (a cold beer — ein is quiet, so who speaks?):
exercises.meaning: ein kaltes Bier = a cold beer (neuter: the adjective echoes -es)
exercises.explanation: das Bier is neuter; ein shows no ending, so the adjective carries the neuter flag: kaltes. The speed set: ein schneller Zug, ein später Zug — ein goes quiet, the adjective speaks.

exercises.prompt: 'Ich trinke den kalt___ Tee.' (the cold tea — masculine accusative):
exercises.meaning: den kalten Tee = the cold tea
exercises.explanation: den already flags the accusative loudly, and the adjective echoes it with -en — the 80/20 ending that covers most real sentences. schwer joins the echo: den schweren Kuchen — the dense cake.

exercises.prompt: Which noun phrase correctly echoes after the quiet article?
exercises.meaning: ein alter Kaffee = an old coffee (masculine nominative)
exercises.explanation: der Kaffee is masculine; ein is endingless in the nominative, so alt picks up the masculine -er exactly as der would wear it.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the phrase pair: 'The old wine is good'
exercises.meaning: Der alte Wein ist gut = the old wine is good

vocab_hints.note: alt + -e: the echo after the loud article der

exercises.explanation: der carries the flag, alte echoes with -e — and predicative gut stays bare, because outside the noun phrase nobody echoes.

summary.outcome: Choose adjective endings after der/die/das vs ein/kein/mein, using the one-flag principle and the 80/20 -en rule.

use_example.german: Der kalte Kaffee ist gut, aber ein kalter Tee ist besser.
use_example.english: The cold coffee is good, but a cold tea is better.

summary.takeaway: One flag per phrase: loud articles speak, quiet ein/kein/mein force the adjective to echo (-er/-es), and -en is the 80% default.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: no article? the adjective goes strong — kaltes Wasser, heißer Tee: the ending does the article's job alone.

alt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *aldaz — the twin of old; the l stayed, the vowel and final d/t report the shift. [wiktionary]

schön.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skauniz — the twin of archaic English sheen 'beautiful'. [wiktionary]

klein.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *klainiz 'clean, fine' — the TRUE twin of English clean; the meaning drifted from 'clean' to 'small'. [wiktionary]

groß.etymology_derivation: T → S/ß shift from Germanic "great". Preserved in English "gross income", "gross national product", and "a gross error" (large, not disgusting).

lang.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *langaz — the identical twin of English long. [wiktionary]

lecker.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German lecker, tied to the verb lecken, to lick, Proto-West Germanic *likkōn; the entry points to English lick as the relative, so the word family is literally about licking. [wiktionary]

neu.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German niuwe, Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, the exact twin of English new; both go back to the same Indo-European root. [wiktionary]

spät.context_phrase: Es ist schon spät in der Nacht.
spät.context_translation: It is already late at night.
spät.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *spādī; only Dutch/Low German cognates — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

schnell.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German snel, Proto-Germanic *snellaz, meaning quick and bold; the exact English cognate is the rare word snell, still heard in northern England and Scotland. [wiktionary]

schwer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *swēraz 'heavy, grave'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

puls.etymology_derivation: From Late Middle High German puls, from Latin pulsus. English pulse comes from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

unfall.context_phrase: Er hatte einen Unfall mit dem Fahrrad.
unfall.context_translation: He had an accident with the bicycle.
unfall.etymology_derivation: Un- (bad) plus Fall (case, fall — exact twin of English fall); literally a bad case, an accident. English accident is Latin, unrelated. [wiktionary]

geschäftsmann.context_phrase: Der Geschäftsmann arbeitet in der Stadt.
geschäftsmann.context_translation: The businessman works in the city.
geschäftsmann.etymology_derivation: Compound of Geschäft (business) and Mann (man), the exact twin of English man; Geschäft is attested from Middle High German gescheft and Old High German giscaft, from the Germanic root family of schaffen and English shape [UNVERIFIED - check]. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
